en: The Inscription on Faith:
The ultimate Way is not difficult; it is only that one dislikes discrimination. If you simply do not harbor likes or dislikes, all will be transparently clear.
A difference of even a hair’s breadth, and heaven and earth are set far apart.
If you wish to attain presence before you, do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance.
To contend with the states of opposition and compliance is the sickness of the mind. Not recognizing the profound essence, you labor in vain to contemplate stillness.
When [the mind] is perfectly identical to the great void, there is neither deficiency nor excess; this is truly due to grasping and rejecting.
Therefore, it is not as [it seems]: do not pursue that which has conditions, and do not dwell in the patience of emptiness.
With a single state of equanimity, all is naturally exhausted. Ceasing movement returns to stillness, yet ceasing further intensifies movement;
to linger only in these two extremes, how could one know this single state?
One kind is not penetrating; in both places, effort is lost. To dispel existence and non-existence is to turn one's back on emptiness;
with many words and much deliberation, things become increasingly inconsistent.
When speech is cut off and deliberation ceases, there is nowhere that is not penetrated, and one returns to the root to attain the essential meaning.
Following after illumination loses the fundamental principle; reflect back for even a moment.
This surpasses the previous emptiness and the current emptiness; all transformations arise from deluded views.
Do not seek the truth, simply allow views to cease. When these two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes confused and loses the mind.
The two arise from the one; even the one cannot be maintained. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Without fault, there are no dharmas; without arising, there is no mind. One can thus follow along until the objects of perception are extinguished.
The object follows along with the subject; the object arises from the subject-object relationship, and the subject arises from the object-subject relationship.
If you wish to know these two segments, they are fundamentally one emptiness.
This single emptiness encompasses both equally, containing all phenomena within it. When neither the refined nor the coarse is seen, how could there be any partiality?
The substance of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult.
With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and increasingly slow. If you grasp at it, you lose its measure; if the mind enters a deviant path, let it be natural.
In its essence, there is no going or staying; follow its nature and you will accord with the Way.
To be carefree is to be free from affliction; to fixate one’s thoughts is to deviate from the truth.
To be mired in dullness is not good; to labor the spirit is not good. What use is there for intimacy or estrangement?
If you wish to enter the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects. If you do not loathe the six sense-objects, you will be identical to Perfect Enlightenment.
The wise are unconditioned; the foolish bind themselves. In the Dharma there is no separate dharma, yet they delusively cling to it with self-attachment.
Using the mind to employ the mind—is this not a great error?
Deluded beings give rise to stillness and agitation; the awakened have neither like nor dislike regarding any of the two extremes.
Do not vainly deliberate; dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—why labor to grasp at gain or loss, right or wrong?
Let them all be cast aside at once. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord;
if the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are as one.
The single suchness is profound in essence; Utterly still, one forgets all conditions. Observing all phenomena as equal, one returns to spontaneity.
Extinguishing that by which they are so— It cannot be compared or likened.
In stillness there is no stillness; in movement there is no movement. Since both are not established, they do not exist.
How can this be? Reaching the ultimate limit, no fixed rules remain;
the mind is opened to equanimity. All conditioned activities have ceased;
doubt is completely purified, and right faith becomes straightened and upright. Nothing is retained, and there is nothing left to be remembered.
Empty clarity is spontaneous; it does not require the exertion of mental effort.
It is beyond the realm of deliberation, difficult for the conscious mind to fathom. Within the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self;
one must urgently seek resonance with it. It is simply called non-duality; in non-duality, all things are identical.
Nothing is not encompassed; the wise of the ten directions all enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor protracted:
a single thought-moment is ten thousand years, and ten thousand years are a single thought-moment. Neither existing nor non-existing, it is before one’s eyes throughout the ten directions.
The smallest is identical to the great; delusion is severed and there is no objective realm.
Extremely great yet slightly small, its boundaries and surface are not seen. Existence is itself non-existence, and non-existence is itself existence.
If it were not thus, one would certainly not need to maintain that "the one is all" and "all is the one";
it is simply by being able to be thus [that this is realized].
What concern is there that it will not be completed? The mind of faith is non-dual.
This non-dual mind of faith cuts off the path of words and speech. It is neither past, future, nor present.
This concludes the *Faith Mind Inscription*.
